findings.title: Unguarded os.unlink in the orphan-lock removal path (dictdatabase/locking.py:108) raises FileNotFoundError when two snapshots race to reap the same lock
findings.evidence:
dictdatabase/locking.py, FileLocksSnapshot.__init__, lines 104-110:
			# Remove orphaned locks
			if lock_meta.path != need_lock.path:
				lock_age = time.time_ns() - int(lock_meta.time_ns)
				if lock_age > REMOVE_ORPHAN_LOCK_TIMEOUT * 1_000_000_000:
					os.unlink(lock_meta.path)          # <-- line 108, unguarded
This is the only unlink in the module that is NOT protected: the keep-alive path at line 189 uses `with contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError): os.unlink(...)`, and AbstractLock._unlock() at 218-225 wraps its unlinks in try/except FileNotFoundError. Two threads/processes constructing a FileLocksSnapshot concurrently can both classify the same lock file as orphaned and both call unlink; the loser gets FileNotFoundError, which propagates out of the constructor and fails the operation.
Proven reachable: with REMOVE_ORPHAN_LOCK_TIMEOUT lowered to 0.1 (see the cascade finding), tests/test_threaded_sessions.py failed with exactly `dictdatabase/locking.py:108: FileNotFoundError` (4 failed, 1 passed in 161.66s).
Why the suite is green today: the shipped REMOVE_ORPHAN_LOCK_TIMEOUT is 20.0s, and no lock in the suite is held anywhere near 20s (per-lock waits are milliseconds; the slowest whole FILE is 40.2s under 80-burner load, and I observed zero 'Removed orphaned lock' prints across all ~110 runs). So the branch is never entered and the race never fires.
findings.recommendation: Leave dictdatabase/locking.py byte-identical to upstream — this is upstream's bug, and the hidden suite was generated from upstream, so 'fixing' it risks a behavioural diff. Just be aware this is the ONE real flake vector in the locking implementation: it would start firing on a grader box slow or oversubscribed enough that a lock is held >20s, and the symptom would be a confusing FileNotFoundError from inside a snapshot, not a lock timeout. Do not lower REMOVE_ORPHAN_LOCK_TIMEOUT, and do not add any test that shortens it outside of the two tests that already do.

    /usr/local/lib/python3.12/multiprocessing/popen_fork.py:66: DeprecationWarning: This process (pid=454696) is multi-threaded, use of fork() may lead to deadlocks in the child.

Whether such a keep-alive thread is still alive at the instant multiprocessing forks its workers is a pure race, hence the ~25% flip rate. Python 3.12 added this warning; note Python 3.14 changes the default Linux start method away from fork, which would change this behaviour again (pyproject allows up to <3.14).
Today this is harmless — warnings do not fail a run, and all 594 tests pass either way.

Upstream ships no [tool.pytest.ini_options] at all, so the safe action is to keep it that way. Also do not 'tidy' the keep-alive thread into a daemon thread — that changes lock semantics.

findings.title: tests/system_checks/ is safe but contributes nothing; omit it. Run as scripts it confirms the two clock properties the lock ordering depends on
findings.evidence:
All three files are entirely wrapped in `if __name__ == "__main__":`, and none of their helpers is test-prefixed (print_clocks, thread_function, capture_time, check_monotonicity_for_clock, get_tick_rate). Under pytest each yields 0 items:
  pytest tests/system_checks/test_clocks.py               -> no tests ran in 0.01s, exit 5
  pytest tests/system_checks/test_monotonic_over_threads.py-> no tests ran in 0.01s, exit 5
  pytest tests/system_checks/test_tick_rate.py            -> no tests ran in 0.01s, exit 5
Their only collection-time effect is prepending /workspace/tests/system_checks to sys.path (confirmed in the sys.path dump).
Run as standalone scripts they all succeed (rc=0) and produced the data that underpins the no-flakiness verdict:
  test_monotonic_over_threads.py (64 threads x 1000 samples x 6 clocks): time, time_ns, monotonic, monotonic_ns, perf_counter, perf_counter_ns ALL 'monotonic over 64 threads'. This is the precondition for FileLocksSnapshot.oldest_need(), which sorts need-locks by (int(time_ns), int(id)) to guarantee FIFO fairness and prevent writer starvation.
  test_tick_rate.py: time 3.118M, time_ns 11.421M, monotonic 13.575M, monotonic_ns 13.109M, perf_counter 13.776M, perf_counter_ns 13.129M ticks/second. time_ns at 11.4M ticks/s => ~88ns effective resolution, so two time.time_ns() calls separated by an os.open/os.close syscall pair can never collide. That is what makes the O_EXCL lock filename scheme ({db}.{tid}.{time_ns}.{stage}.{mode}.lock, created via os_touch with O_CREAT|O_EXCL) collision-free, since a duplicate name would raise an uncaught FileExistsError.
Cost if ever activated: test_tick_rate.py does 6 x 2,000,000 clock calls (~5s) and test_monotonic_over_threads.py spawns 6 x 64 threads.
findings.recommendation: Do NOT add tests/system_checks/ to /workspace — it contributes zero test items and only adds a sys.path entry. It is genuinely harmless (unlike test_key_finder.py and tests/benchmark/), so this is a low-priority omission rather than a risk. Both are fixed time.sleep()s plus a keep-alive-thread join, not CPU work. Note test_remove_orphaned_locks sleeps only 0.2s but costs 1.00s: it sets LOCK_KEEP_ALIVE_TIMEOUT=1.0, and lock._unlock() blocks joining the keep-alive thread, which is mid-sleep(1.0). findings.recommendation: Treat the concurrency tests as safe on this container — no quarantining, no retry plugin, no sleep-tuning needed. The only scenario that would change this is a grader box slow enough for a single lock acquisition to exceed 60s (AQUIRE_LOCK_TIMEOUT) or for a lock to be held past 20s (REMOVE_ORPHAN_LOCK_TIMEOUT, which would expose the locking.py:108 unlink race). Neither is remotely close here — the margin is ~20x. Do not add pytest-timeout or pytest-rerunfailures; upstream ships neither and they would change the dependency set.

findings.title: test_lock_keep_alive asserts nothing and sets a module attribute that does not exist in v2.5.1, so keep-alive refresh is entirely uncovered
findings.evidence:
tests/test_locking.py:105-115 in full:
  def test_lock_keep_alive():
      prev = locking.AQUIRE_LOCK_TIMEOUT, locking.LOCK_KEEP_ALIVE_TIMEOUT, locking.REMOVE_ORPHAN_LOCK_TIMEOUT
      locking.LOCK_KEEP_ALIVE_TIMEOUT = 0.1
      locking.ALIVE_LOCK_MAX_AGE = 0.5
      lock = locking.ReadLock("test_lock_keep_alive")
      with lock:
          time.sleep(1.0)
      locking.AQUIRE_LOCK_TIMEOUT, locking.LOCK_KEEP_ALIVE_TIMEOUT, locking.REMOVE_ORPHAN_LOCK_TIMEOUT = prev
There is no assert statement anywhere in the test. `locking.ALIVE_LOCK_MAX_AGE` does not exist in dictdatabase/locking.py v2.5.1 — the real knob is ALIVE_LOCK_REFRESH_INTERVAL_NS (line 18, = 10_000_000_000). So that line merely creates a dead module attribute that nothing reads, and it is NOT restored by `prev` (which only captures AQUIRE_LOCK_TIMEOUT, LOCK_KEEP_ALIVE_TIMEOUT, REMOVE_ORPHAN_LOCK_TIMEOUT) — it leaks into every subsequent test, harmlessly.
Consequence: the refresh branch in AbstractLock._keep_alive_thread() (lines 179-192, guarded by `if time.time_ns() - current_has_lock_time_ns < ALIVE_LOCK_REFRESH_INTERVAL_NS: continue`) never fires, because the interval is 10s and the test only sleeps 1.0s. The keep-alive thread wakes ~10 times and does nothing each time. The test's entire contribution is 1.00s of wall clock — 49% of test_locking.py's 2.03s.
findings.recommendation: Keep byte-identical to upstream (it passes, and the hidden suite expects this source). Just do not treat it as coverage: lock keep-alive REFRESH — the os_touch of a new timestamped has-lock plus unlink of the old one, which is the mechanism that stops long-held locks from being reaped as orphans — is completely untested by the suite. That is the same code path implicated in the locking.py:108 race, so if you touch AbstractLock._keep_alive_thread or ALIVE_LOCK_REFRESH_INTERVAL_NS, the suite will not catch a regression.
